title: Histograms, distinct counts and extended statistics

videos.script: Lesson 6 showed a plan going wrong because an estimate was wrong. {{recap}} This lesson opens the box the estimate comes from. {{box}} For every column, ANALYZE keeps a short summary of a sample of the table. The commonest values, and how often each one appears. A histogram of the rest. A guess at how many different values there are. And how closely the column follows the order of the rows on disk. {{summary}} The planner turns every condition in a WHERE clause into a fraction of the table. It uses nothing but that summary. {{fraction}} When the summary knows, the fraction is good. Seller 1 has a quarter of all orders, and the planner knows it, because seller 1 is on the list of common values. {{seller}} When the summary cannot say something, the planner assumes. Its favourite assumption is that two columns have nothing to do with each other. A customer in Curitiba is always in Paraná, and the planner multiplies the two fractions anyway. {{curitiba}} The estimate comes out fourteen times too small. {{wrong}} By the end of this lesson you will read pg_stats for any column, work out an estimate by hand, and tell the planner the one fact it cannot learn alone. {{title}}
